concepts.definition: The number of vibrations per second. The higher the frequency, the higher the pitch.
concepts.example: 440 Hz means 440 full vibrations per second, and it is the note La.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking a high frequency means a loud sound; frequency sets how high the pitch is, while intensity sets how loud it is.

concepts.definition: A higher version of the same note, made by doubling the frequency.
concepts.example: La: 440 Hz, one octave higher: 880 Hz.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking an octave means adding a fixed number to the frequency; an octave is not adding, it is multiplying by two.

concepts.definition: An active buzzer always makes the same sound with its own oscillator; a passive buzzer takes its sound from the frequency you send with tone.
concepts.example: To play Do-Re-Mi you use a passive buzzer.
concepts.pitfall: Trying to play notes with an active buzzer; you hear the same pitch at every frequency.

concepts.definition: tone produces a square wave at the given frequency on a pin; if no duration is given, you silence it with noTone.
concepts.example: tone(8, 440, 300) plays La on D8 for 300 ms.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking tone waits until the note is finished; it does not wait, so you need a delay between notes.

concepts.definition: tone and the PWM on D3/D11 use the same timer (Timer2); while tone is playing, analogWrite control on these two pins breaks.
concepts.example: That is why, in the music box, the blue channel only gets 0 or 255 while tone is playing.
concepts.pitfall: Trying to set the brightness of an LED on D11 with analogWrite while tone is playing; you should use D9 or D10.

quiz.prompt: The note Mi is about 330 Hz. How many Hz is the same note one octave higher?
quiz.explanation: Going up one octave means multiplying the frequency by two: 330 × 2 = 660 Hz. The octave rule is multiplication; adding the same fixed number to every note would give the wrong result.

quiz.prompt: A passive buzzer is playing at 440 Hz. About how many milliseconds does one full vibration (HIGH + LOW) take? (Period = 1000 ms / frequency)
quiz.explanation: The period is the inverse of the frequency: 1000 ms / 440 is about 2.27 ms. As the frequency gets bigger the period gets smaller; for 880 Hz it would be about 1.14 ms.

options: Do, Mi, Sol play one after another
The three notes play at the same time, like a chord
Only Sol (392 Hz) is heard, for a short time
No sound comes out at all
quiz.explanation: tone does not wait; the three commands run straight after each other and each new tone replaces the previous one. On the same pin the last call wins, so only 392 Hz (Sol) is heard. To hear the notes one after another you need a delay after each tone. One pin makes one frequency, so a chord is not possible.

options: tone(8, 440, 2000): tone does not take a duration parameter
analogWrite(11, 64): PWM on D11 breaks while tone is playing; the LED should be moved to D9 or D10
pinMode(11, OUTPUT): the pin should be INPUT for tone
delay(2000): you cannot use delay while tone is playing
quiz.explanation: tone and the PWM on D11 use the same Timer2; while tone is playing, brightness control on D11 does not work. The fix is to move the LED to D9 or D10, whose PWM is not affected. tone does take a duration as its third parameter, pinMode does no harm, and the delay is needed here to wait for the note to finish.

quiz.prompt: You wrote a program that plays the C major scale, but all eight notes sound at the same pitch, like a single beep. What is the most likely reason?
options: noTone was used instead of tone
The delay time is too long
The buzzer is set to the active type; an active buzzer makes the same sound at every frequency
quiz.explanation: An active buzzer has its own oscillator and its frequency cannot be changed; the frequency you send with tone does not affect the pitch. The fix is to choose a passive buzzer in the properties panel (or in the real circuit). An array starting at 0 is normal, and delay changes the length, not the pitch.
